paragraphs.text: Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair is a RASopathy. Its features include Noonan syndrome-like facial features, macrocephaly, short neck with redundant skin, short stature often with growth hormone (GH) deficiency, cognitive deficits with hyperactive behavior, cardiac anomalies, and distinctive ectodermal findings. These ectodermal findings include darkly pigmented skin and sparse, thin, slow-growing, easily pluckable hair that shows the features of loose anagen hair (Mazzanti et al., 2003; Cordeddu et al., 2009).

paragraphs.text: Tosti et al. (1991) reported a 4.5-year-old girl with Noonan syndrome and loose anagen hair. Her hair was short and blond, had never been cut, and came out easily when pulled. Scalp biopsy showed marked clefts between fragmented inner root sheaths and irregularly shaped hair shafts.

paragraphs.text: Tosti et al. (1997) described 19 patients with loose anagen hair (LAH), 14 children and 5 adults aged 8 months to 47 years, who were diagnosed at a university medical center from January 1990. One of them, a 5-year-old boy, also had Noonan syndrome. In all patients the trichogram showed mostly anagen hairs (80 to 100%) without sheaths. Pathologic study of hair from 5 patients showed no morphologic abnormalities of the hair follicles other than frequent fragmentation of the inner root sheath, and the authors judged these findings nonspecific and of little diagnostic value. Three adults, each the only affected member of the family, had developed diffuse hair shedding suddenly 1 to 3 years before evaluation. From this the authors concluded that LAH does not arise only in childhood and that adult-onset LAH can be mistaken for telogen hair loss. In 2 families, an affected adult was the parent of an affected child. The authors concluded that LAH may be sporadic, may occur together with developmental or acquired conditions, or, less often, may be familial.

paragraphs.text: Cordeddu et al. (2009) found that 25 individuals with a SHOC2 mutation shared a consistent phenotype, previously termed Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair. Their facial features looked typical of Noonan syndrome and included macrocephaly, high forehead, hypertelorism, ptosis, and low-set, posteriorly rotated ears. They also had short webbed necks and pectus anomalies. Other features were reduced growth, often with proven GH deficiency, cognitive deficits, hyperactive behavior that improved with age in most patients, and easily pluckable, sparse, thin, slow-growing hair. Most patients had darkly pigmented skin with eczema or ichthyosis. Cardiac anomalies were present in most, and mitral valve dysplasia and septal defects were more frequent than in the general Noonan syndrome population. The voice was hypernasal. As newborns or young infants, several patients had been thought to have features suggestive of Costello or cardiofaciocutaneous (CFC) syndrome. In 12 of the mutation-positive patients, microscopic examination of pulled hairs confirmed loose anagen hair.

paragraphs.text: Hoban et al. (2012) reported a male infant with a SHOC2 mutation who presented with fetal distress that required premature delivery at 32 weeks. After birth he had dysmorphic features, edema, hepatosplenomegaly, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and respiratory distress. Echocardiography showed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. The cardiac lesion progressed rapidly, and he was discharged home for palliative care. The authors noted that his cardiac and other findings were not typical of previously reported individuals with this SHOC2 mutation and therefore expanded the clinical phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Patient 1 of Gripp et al. (2013) was a boy born by cesarean section at 38 weeks for macrosomia. The pregnancy was complicated by polyhydramnios and a third-trimester cystic hygroma. He had pyloric stenosis that needed surgical repair, severe failure to thrive that required a gastrostomy at 5 months, mild pulmonic valve stenosis, low axial tone, and motor delay. At 2 years 4 months his OFC was +3 SD, and he had sparse, very fine hair, ptosis, downslanting palpebral fissures, a short neck, hepatosplenomegaly, hemangiomas, and numerous fine wrinkles on the hands. Juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia was suspected at 2 years 3 months, but bone marrow biopsy findings were most consistent with primary myelofibrosis. He died at 2.5 years after a splenectomy performed in preparation for bone marrow transplant.

paragraphs.text: Gripp et al. (2013) found distinctive brain abnormalities in their SHOC2 mutation patients. All 4 patients assessed had relative megalencephaly with enlarged subarachnoid spaces suggestive of benign external hydrocephalus, and a relatively small posterior fossa indicated by a vertical tentorium. Three of the 4 had cerebellar tonsillar ectopia, which the authors attributed to the combination of a large brain and a small posterior fossa. Combining their series with the literature, 3 of 8 patients who had MRI had a Chiari I malformation, and 2 of these malformations appeared to have developed after birth. One patient had periventricular nodular heterotopia. Gripp et al. (2013) also reported myelofibrosis in a 2-year-old with the SHOC2 mutation, the first hematologic neoplasm described in a SHOC2 mutation-positive patient. His bone marrow tested negative for the somatic JAK2 V617F mutation.

paragraphs.text: Cordeddu et al. (2009) chose SHOC2 as the best candidate gene using in silico protein network analysis seeded with known RAS-MAPK mutant proteins. They sequenced SHOC2 in 96 individuals with Noonan syndrome who had no mutations in known genes. They found a heterozygous 4A-G transition, resulting in a ser2-to-gly (S2G) substitution, in 4 unrelated individuals, all of whom were sporadic cases. In the 3 with parental DNA available, the parents did not carry the mutation and paternity was confirmed, showing that the mutation was de novo. The mutation was present in DNA from several tissues, consistent with germline origin. The authors then sequenced SHOC2 in another 410 mutation-negative individuals with Noonan syndrome or a related phenotype and found the same S2G change in 21 of them. It was de novo in all 12 families with parental DNA available. No other disease-associated SHOC2 variant was found, which the authors took as strong evidence that the S2G substitution has a specific pathogenic role. In total, 25 individuals carried the mutation. paragraphs.text: Cordeddu et al. (2009) found that the S2G substitution creates an N-terminal glycine that makes SHOC2 a substrate for N-myristoyltransferase (NMT). In Cos-1 cells, SHOC2 S2G incorporated [3H]-myristic acid, whereas wildtype SHOC2 and a disease-unrelated S2A mutant did not. Wildtype SHOC2 was distributed through the cytoplasm and nucleus in starved cells and moved to the nucleus after EGF stimulation. In contrast, S2G was targeted to the cell membrane in both states. This was confirmed in 293T and Neuro2A cells and by cell fractionation. The NMT inhibitor 2-hydroxymyristic acid reduced or abolished the membrane localization. Even without efficient myristoylation, the mutant did not move to the nucleus. Wildtype SHOC2 and the S2G mutant did not heterodimerize, which ruled out a dominant-negative effect through sequestration of wildtype protein at the membrane. S2G did not significantly change ERK activation in Cos-1 or 293T cells. In Neuro2A neuroblastoma cells, however, it increased EGF-dependent ERK phosphorylation compared with wildtype SHOC2, indicating cell type-specific enhancement of MAPK activation. Citing SHOC2's role as a regulatory subunit of PP1C, the authors proposed that membrane-bound S2G would prolong PP1C-mediated dephosphorylation of RAF1 at ser259 and so sustain RAF1-driven MAPK activation. They also suggested that loose anagen hair reflects disturbed proliferation, survival, or differentiation of epithelial stem cell-derived cells in hair follicles.

Together they form a heterotrimeric holoenzyme that specifically dephosphorylates the inhibitory 'S259' site on RAF kinases (S259 on CRAF, S365 on BRAF), leading to RAF activation. MRAS also acts as a targeting subunit, because the complex must be at the membrane to dephosphorylate RAF efficiently and to regulate the ERK pathway in cells. The predicted structure of SHOC2 closely resembles the A subunit of PP2A, which the authors suggested is a case of convergent structural evolution. Noonan syndrome-associated mutations in SHOC2, MRAS, and PPP1CB invariably promoted formation of the complex among these 3 proteins but did not necessarily increase binding to other interactors. The authors concluded that Noonan syndrome in people with SHOC2, MRAS, or PPP1CB mutations is likely driven at the biochemical level by enhanced formation of this ternary complex.

paragraphs.text: In C. elegans, Cordeddu et al. (2009) found that wildtype SHOC2 could substitute for SUR-8 in a sur-8(rf);let-60(gf) background, but SHOC2 S2G could not. Expressing S2G in let-60(gf) worms did not suppress the multivulva phenotype, which excluded a dominant-negative effect. In wildtype worms, expressing S2G at the early L3 stage caused abnormal vulval development, with protruding vulva, reduced egg laying, and a bag-of-worms phenotype. Myristoylation-tagged wildtype SHOC2 caused the same effects, but untagged wildtype SHOC2 did not. Both S2G and myr::SHOC2 were targeted to the plasma membrane. The defects reflected abnormal vulval morphogenesis rather than altered cell fate specification: P5.p and/or P7.p descendants detached from the cuticle in 17 of 48 S2G larvae and in 10 of 22 myr::SHOC2 larvae.

paragraphs.text: Cordeddu et al. paragraphs.text: Hannig et al. (2014) used RASopathy panel sequencing to identify a heterozygous c.519G-A transition in the SHOC2 gene, resulting in a met173-to-ile (M173I) substitution, in a 5-year-old girl of European ancestry with a mild RASopathy without loose anagen hair.
